transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 10:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maeve Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Park (Redwood SE), Talia Moreno (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (Sable SRE), Priya Singh (Sable Platform), Evan Morales (Sable Security), Carla D'souza (Sable Product)

Summary: follow-up on Feb 28th incident where inference requests saw cascading latency and partial errors during a traffic spike. Walkthrough of RCA, clarifications on mitigations (KV cache eviction, batch sizing, routing/fallback), and agreement on runbook and benchmark plan.

Topics: RCA recap, mitigating short-term and long-term reliability improvements, security/audit implications, dedicated vs hosted routing during peaks, next steps for pilot of Dedicated pool.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maeve (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to do a quick follow up after the incident on Feb 28th, run through the RCA we circulated, answer any Qs, and agree action items. Lucas is gonna walk through the technical findings.
[00:15] Lucas (Redwood SE): Hi all, yeah thanks. Quick reminder: incident timeline in the doc — ~03:12 UTC we saw a traffic burst, simultaneous model size change on customer's end, and then a KV cache thrash that amplified tail latency. I know that phrasing is a bit— the transcription from the logs makes it look more deterministic than it was.
[00:40] Jordan (Sable SRE): sorry can you repeat 'KV cache thrash'? that's the piece we wanna understand clearly, because we saw a lot of pod restarts and liveness probes firing.
[00:50] Lucas: Sure. Basically cache miss rate spiked when a different model version was deployed for a subset of traffic. The cache population logic was eviction-heavy under the combination of high concurrency and small batch sizes. So we had more work per token and the GPU memory pressure caused slower responses and then the autoscaler reacted which caused more scheduling churn. It's a feedback loop.
[01:20] Priya (Sable Platform): The timing matches our deploy at 03:10 where we pushed a config that changed routing to an experimental variant. We didn't expect that to impact cache keys because we thought variants were compatible.
[01:35] Lucas: Right — a subtle difference in tokenizer/embedding prefix meant cache keys didn't match and that effectively invalidated large portions of the prefix cache. Also, the model variant had a slightly different KV layout which made some of our memory heuristics conservative.
[02:00] Evan (Security): From an audit perspective, any risk of data exposure during the failover? We saw logs with partial user inputs in debug traces.
[02:12] Talia (Redwood CSM): We flagged that in the RCA, Evan. The debug traces were internal diagnostic spans; they were masked in prod but a subset were captured in the ephemeral debug bundle during the mitigation window. We've confirmed those traces were not persisted in long-term storage and we've rotated the debug tokens.
[02:30] Carla (Product): Could you share again the specific mitigation steps you took during the incident? The doc lists an emergency rollback, throttling, and then a targeted cache warm-up — is that accurate?
[02:40] Maeve: Yes. Chronology: 03:14 detected rising latency; 03:18 initiated throttling (rate limits tightened for non-critical routes), 03:23 rolled back the experimental variant to restore the cache namespace, 03:30 performed targeted cache rewarm for priority prefixes and increased batch sizing which brought tail latency down.
[03:10] Jordan: The rollback fixed the immediate issue but we still saw a small error spike for ~10 minutes after. Are there recommended changes to prevent recurrence?
[03:20] Lucas: We have a short-term and long-term set. Short-term: enforce token-compatible model variant tagging so cache namespaces remain consistent, add a pre-deploy cache-compatibility check, and automatic fallback to the last-known-good model variant when cache miss rate exceeds threshold. Long-term: richer model metadata in the catalog, smarter KV allocation on mixed-model clusters, and better autoscaler coupling to app-level signals rather than pure pod metrics.
[04:00] Priya: On the pre-deploy check — that sounds actionable. How invasive is it to add to our CI?
[04:10] Lucas: Not too invasive. We added a small shim that hashes tokenizer prefix + model id; it can be run as a lightweight job. We'll provide a script.
[04:20] Maeve: We'll include that script in the RCA repo and put it in the runbook.
[04:26] [05:00] Jordan: There was also mention in the RCA about the Dedicated pool option. Is the idea that we move high-traffic production routes to a reserved capacity so these cross-tenant effects are isolated?
[05:12] Talia: Exactly. Dedicated gives you a predictable GPU pool and reduces noisy neighbor risks. Lucas can speak to tradeoffs.
[05:20] Lucas: Tradeoffs: Dedicated reduces cross-tenant interference and lets you pin a quantization/profile which reduces kernel-selection variance. But it costs more and you need commit sizing. For your workload's peak profile we estimated a 1.6x cost compared to mixed-hosted during low traffic but the predictable tail latency improvements were substantial in our bench.
[05:50] Carla: Do we need to commit now or can we trial Dedicated for a week?
[06:00] Maeve: We can run a short pilot — Redwood supports week-long trials on a dedicated pool for evaluation. We'll set up a timebox and run your sample traffic with our benchmark harness. Lucas will set the test parameters.
[06:15] Lucas: I'll scope a test: 48-hour soak with stepped traffic up to your observed peak, with and without payload variance, and capture latency distributions and KV miss rates.
[06:30] Evan: On compliance — any difference in logs/audit for Dedicated vs Hosted? We need consistent audit trails and KMS controls.
[06:40] Talia: Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS and we can extend audit retention. The security docs I shared last week cover that; I'll re-share the link.
[06:55] [08:00] Jordan: A question on autoscaler: during the incident pods were briefly stuck in pending then killed. Could that be kube-scheduler pressure or our taints/tolerations?
[08:12] Lucas: From our traces, the primary cause was GPU memory pressure leading to OOM-like behavior in the runtime, the scheduler then tried to evict and re-create. There were also spot preemption events on the infra side that caused additional churn. We recommend a combo of node-level overprovisioning and more conservative readiness/liveness thresholds for heavy inference pods.
[08:40] Priya: We'll check our node pool config. Also can you clarify 'spot preemption' — are you saying your hosted infra used spot instances?
[08:50] Maeve: For your current hosted tier yes, we run a mix for cost efficiency — spikes can coincidentally line up with preemptions; Dedicated avoids that.
[09:10] [12:00] Jordan: About the debug traces — you said they were ephemeral and rotated. We still want to ensure no PII was recorded. Can you confirm the fields masked?
[09:25] Talia: We did an audit. Inputs were redacted in the stored traces. The ephemeral debug bundle contained partial user text for a small subset; we used automated redaction and manual review and then purged the bundle. I can send the purge confirmation.
[09:45] Evan: Please do. We'll need it for our compliance ticket.
[09:50] Maeve: We'll send the purge confirmation and the sanitized bundle summary.
[10:10] [15:00] Lucas: A technical note on batch sizing — we observed your client-side requests had small batch sizes because of interactive latency constraints. However, small batches at high concurrency increase per-token overhead. One mitigant is adaptive batching on the edge, or aggregating similar requests for a short micro-window (10-50ms) — trades a hair of latency for big improvements in throughput and lower tail.
[15:40] Carla: Our product team is sensitive to latency; what would that trade look like in percentiles?
[15:50] Lucas: Typical: P50 unaffected, P95 improves sometimes by ~20-30% for high token workloads, P99 improves even more because batching smooths GPU kernel amortization. We'll share synthetic curves.
[16:10] Jordan: Can Redwood's routing prioritize routes during spikes so critical traffic gets cache-warmed earlier?
[16:20] Maeve: Yes — we have routing policies that can pin certain routes to pre-warmed nodes or bump priority; that's part of the Dedicated strategy but we can also configure it on hosted for key routes.
[16:40] [22:00] Priya: For immediate remediation, what's the simplest change we can make in 24 hours?
[22:10] Lucas: I think add the pre-deploy cache-compatibility check in your CI and a temporary rule to route critical routes to a small, warm pool or increase batch sizing in your client for the spike window. Those are low-friction.
[22:45] Maeve: We'll send the CI script and a playbook entry for the runbook so your on-call has clear steps.
[23:10] Jordan: Ok that sounds good. For the RCAs we got, is there an explicit timeline for the long-term platform changes?
[23:20] Talia: We outlined a roadmap: metadata/catalog work and autoscaler coupling are Q2 initiatives; we can prioritize the cache-compat check and fallback logic earlier if you want to be on a faster cadence.
[23:45] Carla: Yes please prioritize fallback logic if possible.
[24:00] Lucas: We'll scope the fallback work as a sprint-level patch — likely a few weeks to implement and test. I'll estimate and include in the follow-up.
[24:20] [30:00] Evan: One last security ask — if we trial Dedicated, can we run it inside our VPC with SAML SSO for console access?
[30:12] Talia: Yes; Redwood Private/Dedicated supports SAML SSO integrations and VPC peering for Dedicated clusters. We'll map the exact SSO flow and required config.
[30:40] Maeve: We'll include an appendix in the follow-up that lists required network config and SSO metadata fields.
[30:55] [40:00] Lucas: Quick note on telemetry — during the incident our tracer sampling was low at that time which made debug harder. We'll propose increased sampling for critical routes during pilot windows.
[40:10] Jordan: Agreed. We'll accept increased sampling for limited windows.
[40:25] Maeve: Ok, final recap then next steps.
[40:30] Maeve: Redwood action items: send updated RCA (with sanitized logs), CI pre-deploy cache-compatibility script, playbook runbook entry, schedule Dedicated pilot and benchmark plan, share purge confirmation for debug bundle. Customer action items: provide pod logs/spans for 02/28 window, confirm pilot dates and provide sample traffic.
[41:00] Carla: We'll aim to have logs by 03/05 and pick pilot dates by EOD 03/06.
[41:10] Jordan: Yes logs on 03/05.
[41:20] Maeve: Great. We'll follow up in a calendar invite and attach the proposed benchmark spreadsheet.
[41:35] Lucas: I'll also include synthetic curves for batch sizing tradeoffs and a short runbook snippet for throttling thresholds.
[41:50] Evan: We'll open a compliance ticket referencing the purge confirmation once we get the doc.
[41:58] Talia: I'll send the security appendix and the SAML/VPC checklist.
[42:10] Maeve: Thanks everyone — appreciate the quick coordination. We'll circulate materials and sync early next week.
[42:30] [End]
